[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"MySQL Binary Log (Binlog) Formats and Synchronization Tutorial"},{"order":2,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction to MySQL Binary Logs"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"The MySQL Binary Log (binlog) contains events that describe database changes, such as table creation operations or changes to table data. It also contains statements that potentially make changes. The binary log has two primary purposes: replication and data recovery. Understanding binlog formats and synchronization settings is critical for maintaining high availability and consistency in distributed MySQL architectures."},{"order":4,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding Binlog Formats"},{"order":5,"type":"paragraph","text":"MySQL supports three distinct logging formats: Statement-Based Replication (SBR), Row-Based Replication (RBR), and Mixed-Based Replication (MBR). Each format impacts performance, disk space, and replication safety differently."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Statement-Based Replication (SBR): SQL statements that modify data are logged to the binlog. It is compact and uses less disk space, but can cause non-deterministic issues (e.g., using NOW() or UUID())."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Row-Based Replication (RBR): Changes to individual rows are logged. This format guarantees replication safety and handles non-deterministic functions easily, but generates significantly larger log volumes."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Mixed-Based Replication (MBR): Uses SBR by default, but automatically switches to RBR when MySQL detects statements that cannot be safely replicated using statements alone."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Configuring the Binlog Format"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can configure the binlog format globally via the MySQL configuration file (my.cnf or my.ini) or dynamically using the SET statement. To set the format to ROW, use the following configuration:"},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"[mysqld]
binlog_format = ROW
log_bin = mysql-bin"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"Alternatively, you can change the format dynamically at runtime for the current session or globally using SQL commands."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"SET GLOBAL binlog_format = 'ROW';"},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Binlog Synchronization and Durability"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Data durability and crash recovery depend heavily on how often the binary log is synchronized to the disk. The sync_binlog system variable controls this behavior. Setting sync_binlog = 1 provides the highest level of durability because the binlog is synchronized to disk after every write, but it incurs a performance penalty due to frequent disk I/O."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"[mysqld]
sync_binlog = 1"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"If sync_binlog is set to 0, MySQL relies entirely on the operating system to flush the binary log to disk, which is faster but risks data loss in the event of a power outage or unexpected server crash."},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Verifying Configuration and Status"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"To verify your current binlog settings, use the SHOW VARIABLES command in your MySQL client."},{"order":20,"type":"code","text":"SHOW VARIABLES LIKE '%binlog%';
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'sync_binlog';"},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"By balancing binlog formats (such as preferring ROW or MIXED) with safe synchronization settings (sync_binlog = 1), you ensure that your MySQL replication topology remains robust, deterministic, and disaster-recoverable."}]
